Family Health

Keratin hair treatments: benefits, ingredients and safety questions

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A smoothing treatment may make hair easier to style, but the word “keratin” says little about the safety of the complete formula. Look at the ingredients, heat and exposure before deciding.

What a keratin treatment actually is

Keratin is one of the proteins that gives hair, nails and skin their structure. A salon service sold as a keratin treatment is a cosmetic smoothing process, often involving a liquid product, blow-drying and a hot flat iron. Products and methods differ; the name does not identify one standard formula.

Some cosmetic keratin ingredients come from animal materials such as wool or feathers. Ask the manufacturer about ingredient origin if this matters to you. More importantly for safety, check the complete formula: a familiar protein on the front label does not tell you which other chemicals will be heated during the service.

The benefits: and what it cannot promise

People choose these treatments to reduce frizz, increase shine, soften the appearance of curls or make styling easier. Results depend on the starting texture, prior chemical damage, formulation and aftercare. The change may last for weeks or months, but a lasting result is not guaranteed.

Smoother hair can look healthier without being permanently repaired. A treatment does not create new follicles or prove that hair will grow faster. Less breakage can help hair retain length, while excessive heat or unsuitable chemicals can have the opposite effect. Discuss your actual aim (less frizz, easier detangling or a different curl pattern) before agreeing to a process that may change your hair substantially.

Why formaldehyde is a concern

Some smoothing products contain formaldehyde or ingredients that can release it, particularly when heated. The gas can irritate the eyes, nose, throat, skin and lungs. Symptoms may include watery or burning eyes, headache, coughing, wheezing, nausea or a rash. People with asthma or a previous sensitivity may react more strongly.

Formaldehyde is a recognised human carcinogen. The risk from an exposure depends on factors such as amount and duration; one salon visit cannot be translated into a personal cancer prediction. Nor is an occasional customer automatically protected from an acute reaction. Stylists may face repeated exposure across many treatments.

What product-testing studies found

A South African study published in 2014 examined seven commercial keratin-type straightening brands marketed there in 2012. Six contained measured formaldehyde concentrations of about 0.96–1.4%; five of those carried formaldehyde-free labels. This was a small survey of particular products at a particular time, not an estimate for every current product worldwide.

A separate 2011 study investigated four professional straightening products and measured formaldehyde exposure during use. It found that some treatments could produce concentrations meeting or exceeding occupational exposure limits, including products marketed as formaldehyde-free. Together, these studies help explain concern about misleading labelling, but cannot certify whether a bottle on sale today is safe.

Why a percentage is not a simple safety guarantee

The percentage of a chemical in a liquid and its concentration in the air are different measurements. Airborne formaldehyde is often reported in parts per million, or ppm. Heating, ventilation, the amount used and several treatments running at once can change what a customer or worker breathes.

The older product study compared its results with a 0.2% cosmetic benchmark. That should not be read as permission to heat any straightening product below that percentage. Occupational limits also use specified averaging times and are not a promise of no symptoms for every person. You cannot judge a salon’s exposure level from a reassuring number on a bottle, an open window or the absence of a strong smell.

Reading “formaldehyde-free” and other label claims

Look beyond the service name and ask for the product’s ingredient list and safety data sheet. Names associated with formaldehyde include formalin, methanal, methylene glycol and methanediol. Some ingredients can release formaldehyde under use conditions even if that word is absent from the front label.

Not every smoothing treatment contains formaldehyde, and formaldehyde is not a required ingredient in every effective hair-styling method. However, “natural,” “organic” or “formaldehyde-free” does not establish that all other ingredients and heated emissions are harmless. A long list of vaguely similar chemical names is not a reliable home safety test; the specific product and how it is used matter.

A newer concern: glyoxylic acid and kidney injury

Glyoxylic acid has been used in some straightening products, including alternatives to formaldehyde-based formulas. Following reports and research, the French agency ANSES concluded in 2025 that it very likely played a causal role in reported acute kidney injuries and advised against using products containing it while regulatory assessment proceeded.

Reported symptoms after straightening included lower-back or abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and feeling unwell, sometimes within hours. If these develop after a treatment, seek prompt medical assessment and mention the product exposure. Keep the packaging or a photograph of its ingredients. This concern is another reason that removing one hazardous ingredient does not automatically make a substitute safe.

Questions to ask before booking

Request the exact brand, product name and ingredient list before the appointment, not after the solution is on your hair. Ask whether it contains formaldehyde-related ingredients or glyoxylic acid, whether it is intended to be heated and what current local restrictions apply. A salon should be able to explain its process and respond to a safety question without dismissing it.

Also discuss previous bleach, dye, relaxers, breakage and scalp problems, along with the likely texture change, maintenance, cost and how long the appointment may take. A patch or strand test cannot rule out an inhalation hazard or kidney injury. If the formula or safety information is unavailable, postpone the service rather than relying on a marketing claim.

Extra considerations for salon workers

A stylist’s exposure can accumulate through repeated work, even when they are not receiving the treatment themselves. Employers need appropriate hazard information, ventilation and protective measures, with exposure assessment where required. Simply wearing ordinary gloves or a loose face covering does not solve an airborne chemical problem.

Ask for the safety data sheets and training relevant to the products used at work. Report symptoms and obtain occupational-health advice about controls or alternative duties when needed. If you are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, discuss the actual job tasks and frequency of exposure; the salon’s general reputation is not an exposure assessment.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Hair treatments are not all the same exposure. Evidence about routine colouring cannot automatically be applied to a heated straightening service. Reproductive studies among hairdressers involve different products, hours and working conditions, making individual risks difficult to separate. Some occupational formaldehyde studies have raised miscarriage concerns.

Postponing a nonessential chemical smoothing treatment during pregnancy is a reasonable precaution, especially when the ingredients or emissions are uncertain. If a treatment has already happened, that does not establish that harm occurred: discuss the product and any symptoms with your maternity clinician or a teratology information service.

Small absorption through healthy skin is reassuring for many ordinary hair-care products during breastfeeding, but it does not prove every heated straightener safe. Ask about the specific exposure. Do not stop breastfeeding automatically because you had a salon service; obtain individual advice if there is a concern.

Lower-exposure ways to manage frizz and dryness

A suitable conditioner, gentler detangling, careful towel drying and fewer high-heat styling sessions can improve manageability without a chemical straightening service. Choose a washing routine that suits your scalp and hair texture; avoiding shampoo indefinitely is not a treatment for damaged hair.

Some people find small amounts of a suitable hair oil or a formulated leave-in product useful. Olive, argan, coconut, sunflower oils and shea-based products are options people use, not interchangeable cures or proof of hair growth. Stop a product that irritates your skin. Homemade baking-soda, vinegar or clay routines are not necessary to restore keratin, and “natural” ingredients can still cause problems.

Avoid treating hot irons as risk-free alternatives: limit heat and follow appropriate tool instructions. Persistent shedding, bald patches, scalp inflammation or ongoing breakage deserves dermatology advice rather than repeated smoothing treatments or unproven supplements.

If symptoms develop during or after treatment

Tell the stylist immediately if your eyes or throat burn, you cough, feel dizzy or develop a rash. Stop the exposure and move to fresh air when it is safe to do so. Do not stay through worsening symptoms just to finish the service.

Breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or a severe allergic reaction needs emergency care. Persistent irritation or a chemical burn needs medical advice; new abdominal or lower-back pain with vomiting after straightening also warrants prompt assessment. Share the product name, timing and ingredient information, and report suspected adverse effects through your local cosmetic-safety system.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cosmetic smoothing is not proof of permanent repair or faster hair growth.

Formaldehyde-related emissions and glyoxylic-acid kidney concerns require attention to the actual product.

How BeMama can help

Ask for the complete product information before booking and choose a lower-exposure routine when the answers are unclear.

When to seek help

Stop exposure if symptoms develop. Breathing difficulty or chest pain needs emergency help; pain with vomiting after straightening needs prompt assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Products sold as keratin treatments do not all have the same formula.
  • Some benefits are cosmetic and temporary.
  • Formaldehyde-free is not a guarantee of safety.
  • Pregnancy and workplace exposure need product-specific consideration.
  • Gentle conditioning and less heat are practical alternatives.

Frequently asked questions

Does a keratin treatment make hair grow faster?

It has not been established as a way to speed follicle growth. Smoother hair or reduced breakage may change its appearance and retained length, but that is different from growing new hair.

Is a formaldehyde-free label enough?

No. Past testing found misleading labels, and other ingredients can have their own hazards. Ask for the complete formula and safety information rather than relying on the front label.

Which ingredient names should I ask about?

Formaldehyde, formalin, methylene glycol, methanediol and methanal are relevant names. Also ask specifically about glyoxylic acid. This is not a complete screening list or a guarantee that unlisted alternatives are safe.

Does a low formaldehyde percentage make heating a product safe?

Not by itself. Liquid concentration and airborne exposure are different, and heating and ventilation affect what is inhaled. A generic cosmetic percentage is not a personal safety threshold.

Can a treatment damage my kidneys?

Acute kidney injury has been reported with some glyoxylic-acid straighteners. Seek prompt care for new abdominal or lower-back pain, vomiting or significant illness afterward and show the clinician the product details.

Is one appointment harmless if I do not work in a salon?

No one can promise that. Repeated occupational exposure is a particular concern, but acute irritation or other adverse effects can occur in a customer after a single treatment.

Should I have chemical smoothing while pregnant?

Consider postponing a nonessential service, especially when the ingredients or emissions are unclear. Discuss a specific planned or past exposure with your maternity clinician or a teratology information service.

Must I stop breastfeeding after a keratin service?

Not automatically. Obtain advice about the exact product and any symptoms. Evidence about ordinary hair care does not establish the safety of every heated smoothing formula.

Can I make an equivalent treatment with kitchen ingredients?

There is no need to use vinegar, baking soda or clay to replace hair keratin. Choose gentle, hair-type-appropriate cleansing and conditioning; stop anything that irritates your scalp.

What should I do if I start wheezing in the salon?

Stop the treatment and move away from the exposure safely. Breathing difficulty needs urgent emergency help. Tell the treating team the product name and when the symptoms began.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
